stories.headline: Shoppers spent less, so markets now bet the Fed will wait
stories.dek: July U.S. retail sales fell more than expected, and traders now think the U.S. central bank is less likely to raise interest rates in September.
stories.caveman: Imagine the United States as a giant store. Last month, people bought less stuff than experts thought they would. That is called retail sales. The number dropped 0.6 percent in July. People also said they feel worse about money. A survey of how Americans feel about the economy fell to 51, which is a gloomy score. Why does a shop matter to the whole world? Because the U.S. has a group of officials who set the price of borrowing money. That group is the Federal Reserve, often just called the Fed. When the Fed raises interest rates, loans, houses, and credit cards get more expensive. That can slow price rises, but it can also hurt jobs. Before this week, many traders thought the Fed would raise rates again in mid-September. After the weak shopping numbers, most now think the Fed will hold still. Stocks had just hit a record high, then slipped a little on Friday. Gold went up. The U.S. dollar went down a bit. The story is simple: people are spending less, so the money bosses may stop tightening the screws.
stories.why_it_matters: About seven-tenths of the U.S. economy is people buying things. If they keep pulling back, companies make less money and stock markets can fall. But if weaker shopping also cools inflation, the Fed can leave rates alone, which many investors like. The catch is that prices are still rising faster than the Fed wants, and oil from the Iran war could push them up again.
stories.camps: Investors who own stocks mostly want the Fed to pause, because cheap borrowing helps share prices. Some economists warn that wishing for weak shopping is dangerous: if people stop buying for too long, profits and jobs suffer. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has not said what he will do next. The White House wants cheaper living costs for voters before November elections. Critics say the Fed should stay independent and follow the data, not politics.
stories.image_alt: Cargo and other ships on a hazy horizon at sea

terms.explain: A monthly count of how much money people in a country spend in stores and online. If the number falls, it often means households are nervous or poorer.
The main bank of the United States. It does not serve regular customers. Its job is to keep prices from rising too fast and to keep as many people working as it can.
The extra money you pay to borrow. If the Fed raises this rate, mortgages, car loans, and credit cards get more expensive.
When the same basket of food, rent, and fuel costs more than it did last year. A little inflation is normal. A lot of it hurts people who live on wages.
A poll that asks regular people how they feel about their money and the future. A falling score means people are worried.
A list of 500 big U.S. companies. When people say 'the market hit a record,' they often mean this list went higher than ever.
The return you get for lending money to the U.S. government. When yields rise, borrowing gets costlier for everyone.
A score that shows whether the U.S. dollar is strong or weak against other currencies. A weaker dollar can make imports cost more.
A metal people buy when they are scared of war, inflation, or messy politics. Its price often rises when other assets look risky.
A yearly meeting of central bankers in Wyoming, U.S. The Fed chair often gives a speech there that moves markets. This year's meeting is August 27 to 29.
The current head of the Federal Reserve. He has not clearly said whether rates will go up in September.
Price rises after you take out food and energy, which jump around a lot. The Fed watches this to see the deeper trend.
A huge adding-up of everything a country makes and sells in a year. If GDP shrinks, that is a recession.
One-hundredth of 1 percent. If a bond yield rises 5 basis points, it went from, say, 4.68 percent to 4.73 percent.
A measure of what companies pay for goods before they sell them to you. If this jumps, store prices often follow.

stories.headline: Oil jumps again as the Hormuz bottleneck stays almost shut
stories.dek: Brent crude rose above $88 a barrel on Friday, U.S. gasoline is about 29 percent more expensive than a year ago, and almost no oil tankers are getting through the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.caveman: A huge share of the world's oil used to squeeze through a narrow sea lane between Iran and Oman. That lane is the Strait of Hormuz. Think of it as a one-lane bridge that most of the neighborhood must cross to get fuel. Since the United States and Israel started a war with Iran in late February, that bridge has been almost closed. On Friday, ship-trackers saw only two vessels go through. In peacetime, more than 130 ships a day used it. Because less oil is moving, the price of a barrel of Brent crude, a world oil benchmark, settled at $88.52, up more than a dollar on the day. In the United States, a gallon of gasoline averaged about $4.08, up 29 percent from a year earlier. President Donald Trump told a crowd that paying 'a tiny little bit more' at the pump is the cost of stopping Iran from getting a nuclear bomb. Iran says it, not America, will decide when the strait opens. A tanker owned by Abu Dhabi's oil company was hit in the waterway on Friday. Nobody on board was hurt. Households from Taipei to Texas feel this as higher fuel, food shipping, and airfares.
stories.why_it_matters: Energy is in almost everything you buy. When oil stays high, inflation stays sticky, and central banks find it harder to cut or even hold rates. East Asia, including Taiwan, imports most of its fuel, so a long Hormuz squeeze hits factory costs and household bills. Saudi Aramco has said the world has already lost a huge amount of oil supply since the war began.
stories.camps: Trump and his Treasury secretary say higher U.S. gas prices are worth it to crush Iran's economy and block a nuclear weapon. Vice President JD Vance has also said cheap oil for Americans is goal number one, which is a slightly different pitch. Iran says the U.S. has already lost and must accept defeat. Oil-importing countries in Asia and Europe want the strait reopened for trade. Climate and left-leaning critics say a fossil-fuel war is making living costs worse for ordinary people while oil companies profit.
stories.image_alt: Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran

terms.explain: A narrow sea passage at the mouth of the Persian Gulf. Before the war, about one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil and a lot of gas went through it.
A standard type of oil used to set world prices. When people say 'oil is at $88,' they often mean Brent.
The main U.S. oil price marker. It usually sits a few dollars below Brent.
The unit used to sell oil. One barrel is 42 U.S. gallons, or about 159 liters.
The fuel most U.S. cars burn. Americans talk about the price per gallon the way others talk about the price of rice.
A giant ship built to carry oil or other bulk goods. Hitting one can spill fuel and scare other ships away.
The state oil company of Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates. One of its tankers was attacked in Hormuz on Friday.
When ships or missiles stop other ships from going in or out of a port or sea lane. It is a way to choke an enemy's trade without occupying the land.
A bomb that uses splitting or fusing atoms. It can destroy a city. The U.S. says it went to war to stop Iran from building one. Iran says it does not want one.
A written promise that is not quite a full treaty. The U.S. and Iran signed one in June. A 60-day talk window from that deal ends Monday with little progress.
A radio box on a ship that tells the world where it is. Some ships turn it off to sneak through dangerous waters.
A company that watches oil ships from space and port data. Analysts use it to see if oil is actually moving.
When everyday prices rise. Fuel is a big part of that, because trucks, ships, and farms all burn it.
The U.S. official in charge of government money and many sanctions. He has promised new financial pressure on Iran.
The number-two person in the U.S. government. He has been told to lead talks to end the Iran war and has said cheap oil is his top goal.

stories.headline: Japan's central bank looks ready to raise rates in September
stories.dek: Three people familiar with the Bank of Japan's thinking told Reuters it may hike as soon as mid-September and then raise rates faster than twice a year.
stories.caveman: Japan is a rich country that, for a long time, kept the cost of borrowing almost at zero so people and companies would spend. That extra-easy money made the Japanese yen cheap. A cheap yen means Japanese goods are bargains abroad, but it also makes oil, food, and imported parts expensive at home. Last month Japan and the United States even teamed up to buy yen, hoping to stop it from falling. It did not fix the problem. The yen is still near 160 per dollar, a level that often scares Tokyo. So Japan's central bank, the Bank of Japan, is now thinking about charging more for money. Sources told Reuters a hike could come at the September 17–18 meeting. The bank already lifted its main rate to 1 percent in June, the highest in 31 years. Markets now put the chance of another September hike around 76 to 80 percent. If Japan keeps raising rates, money that had been borrowed cheaply in yen and invested elsewhere may flow home. That can shake stocks, bonds, and currencies worldwide, including in Asia.
stories.why_it_matters: Japan is the world's fourth-largest economy and a huge lender. When it raises rates, global investors often sell other assets to pay back cheap yen loans. Taiwan and other Asian exporters watch the yen because a stronger yen can change who wins in electronics and cars. Faster Japanese hikes also signal that war-driven oil and AI-driven demand are pushing prices up even in a country famous for cheap money.
stories.camps: The Bank of Japan says it must look at inflation risks, a weak yen, and very easy financial conditions. Some Japanese households want a stronger yen so imports cost less. Exporters and the old cheap-money camp worry that faster hikes could hurt growth. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has nudged Tokyo to do more, which some Japanese officials resent as outside pressure. Markets have already priced in a September move, so a delay could look like a broken promise.
stories.image_alt: Pedestrians walk past the Bank of Japan headquarters in Tokyo

terms.explain: Japan's central bank. It sets the country's main interest rate, the way the Fed does in the United States.
When a central bank makes borrowing more expensive on purpose, to cool prices or support its currency.
Japan's money. If it takes more yen to buy one U.S. dollar, the yen is weak. A weak yen makes foreign goods cost more in Japan.
When a government spends huge sums to buy or sell its own money, hoping to change the exchange rate. Japan and the U.S. did this together last month.
The head of the Bank of Japan. He has said the bank might speed up rate rises if money is still too easy.
The Goldilocks interest rate that neither heats up nor cools down the economy. Japan's officials think theirs sits somewhere between about 1.1 and 2.5 percent.
Extra-cheap or extra-plentiful money that a central bank pumps out to get people spending. Japan ran a huge version of this for about a decade and started exiting in 2024.
What factories pay for inputs. Japan is watching these, plus what people expect future prices to do.
Borrowing cheap yen and investing the money in higher-paying assets elsewhere. When Japan raises rates, this trade can unwind fast and shake markets.
America's top finance official. He has publicly pushed Japan to do more about the weak yen.
One-hundredth of a percent. Traders use it when talking about small rate moves.
The return on lending to Japan's government for five years. It has jumped as people bet on rate hikes.
How many yen one dollar buys. Near 160, many traders expect Tokyo to step in again.
What people think prices will do next year. If they expect more inflation, they may demand higher wages, which can make inflation real.

stories.headline: Apple wants a 15 percent cut even when you pay outside the App Store
stories.dek: After the U.S. Supreme Court refused to pause the case, Apple told a California court it still wants a fee on purchases that start in an iPhone app but finish on the web.
stories.caveman: If you have an iPhone, you usually buy extra lives, songs, or subscriptions through Apple's shop, the App Store. Apple has long taken a big slice of that money, often 15 or 30 percent. A game company called Epic Games, which makes Fortnite, sued. It said Apple was using its power over the iPhone to block cheaper ways to pay. A judge later said Apple had to let apps link out to the regular internet so people could pay there. Apple then tried to charge 27 percent on those outside payments and made the links hard to use. The judge was not happy. On Thursday the Supreme Court, America's highest court, refused Apple's request to freeze the fight. So Apple had to show its new plan. It now proposes a 15 percent cut on standard apps, 10 percent for some partner programs and subscription renewals, and 5 percent for small developers. Apple says it built the phones and the tools, so it deserves a fee. Epic and many app makers say a tax on a link is still a tax. Google's Android shop charges similar outside-link fees, which Apple pointed to as proof its plan is normal.
stories.why_it_matters: This is about who controls the door to a billion phones. If Apple keeps a cut on web payments, prices for apps, news, and games stay higher. If the court forces a real opening, smaller companies and users may pay less, and Apple's very profitable services business could shrink. The case also shows how U.S. courts, not just Congress, are rewriting Big Tech rules.
stories.camps: Apple says the fee pays for security, privacy tools, and the cost of running iOS. Epic and many developers say Apple is a gatekeeper that should not charge for a sale it did not process. The Trump administration has mixed feelings about Big Tech: it likes U.S. champions abroad but also likes to look tough on coastal corporations. Consumer advocates and the left generally want lower fees and more competition. Some conservatives care more about speech on the App Store than about the percentage cut.
stories.image_alt: Apple CEO Tim Cook waves onstage in front of a glowing Apple logo

terms.explain: The only official place to download apps on an iPhone. Apple sets the rules and usually takes a cut of sales.
The slice of money Apple wants from a sale. Fifteen percent means Apple keeps $15 of every $100 you spend.
A U.S. game company that sued Apple. It wanted players to pay Epic directly instead of through Apple.
When a powerful company uses its position to block rivals, not just to make a better product. That can be illegal under U.S. law.
A button inside an app that sends you to a website to pay. Apple used to ban these. A court said it cannot.
The highest court in the United States. Its nine justices can stop or allow lower-court fights. On Thursday it refused to pause this one.
When someone ignores a judge's order. Epic says Apple did this with the 27 percent fee and harsh link rules. That question is still alive.

terms.term: U.S. District Court of Northern California
terms.explain: The trial court in San Francisco's region that has been hearing the Epic case for years.
Apple's cheaper track for smaller app makers. Under the new plan they would pay 5 percent on outside-link sales.
When a monthly or yearly payment rolls over. Apple now says it would take 10 percent on those if you pay off-store.
Google's app shop for Android phones. It also charges for some outside-link sales, which Apple used as a comparison.
The operating system that runs iPhones and iPads. Apple controls it tightly.
Buying something while you are already inside an app, like extra storage or a magazine month.
The part of Apple that makes money from the App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, and similar, not from selling hardware.
A person or company that writes apps. They have long complained that Apple's cut is too high.

stories.headline: Apple trained its own China AI with Alibaba's help
stories.dek: Reuters reports Apple built a China-only large language model with Alibaba, after Beijing registered Apple as the first foreign firm allowed to offer its own generative AI to mainland users.
stories.caveman: Apple wants the same smart writing and voice tricks on iPhones in China that it already sells in the U.S. Those tricks are called Apple Intelligence. They run on a large language model, which is a computer program trained on huge piles of text so it can chat, summarize, and write. China does not allow U.S. models like ChatGPT to serve the public. Every AI that talks to Chinese users must be registered with a government internet office and pass a content check. Until this summer, every approved model was Chinese. Reuters now says Apple secretly trained its own China model with help from Alibaba, a giant Chinese tech firm. Apple had already planned to plug in Alibaba's Qwen model and some Baidu tech. Building its own model would give Apple more control. The service is expected to reach Chinese iPhones in the coming months after a software update. Apple and Alibaba did not comment. Critics will ask what the model is forbidden to say. Supporters will say this is the only way a U.S. phone company can compete in China at all.
stories.why_it_matters: China is still one of Apple's biggest markets. If Siri and writing tools feel dumb there while Huawei and others ship local AI, Apple loses sales. The deal also shows how U.S. tech now splits in two: one product for most of the world, another that must obey Beijing's speech rules. For Taiwan and other Asian users, it is a reminder that the AI race is also a political filter.
stories.camps: Apple presents this as following local law so customers get features. U.S. hawks say helping train a model under Chinese censorship hands Beijing leverage and normalizes two internets. China says every country regulates AI and that foreign firms must follow Chinese rules, just as Chinese apps must follow U.S. rules. Privacy advocates worry users will not know which political answers were blocked. Investors mostly care whether Apple Intelligence finally ships in China and stops the sales slide.
stories.image_alt: Apple logo on a processor chip under red and blue lighting

terms.explain: A computer program trained on enormous amounts of text so it can write, translate, and answer questions in human-like language.
Apple's brand name for on-phone AI features such as writing tools and a smarter Siri.
A huge Chinese internet company, a bit like Amazon plus a cloud-computing firm. Its AI family is called Qwen.
Alibaba's public AI model. Apple had already said it would use Qwen inside China-version Apple Intelligence.
Another big Chinese tech company, best known for search. Reuters has said some of its technology may also sit inside Apple's China AI.
The government office that decides which AI chatbots may go live in China. It registered Apple's service in July.
Software that creates new text, pictures, or code instead of just finding old files. ChatGPT is the famous example.
A required test in China. The model must refuse or reframe answers the state does not want, for example on politics or history.
An AI a company owns and trains itself, rather than renting someone else's. Apple is the first foreign firm China has cleared to offer one.
When the AI runs on your phone instead of a faraway server. Apple likes this for privacy. In China, the exact setup is not fully public.
The U.S. company behind ChatGPT. Its models are not allowed as a public service in mainland China.
The voice helper on iPhones. Apple Intelligence is meant to make it much smarter.
Apple's phone software. The China AI features are expected after a future iOS update, not necessarily today.
Using both Apple's own model and Chinese partner models at once, so Apple can pass rules and still keep some control.
Alibaba's chairman. In 2025 he said Apple chose Alibaba after talking to several Chinese firms.

stories.headline: Trump opens his war chest as Republicans fear losing Congress
stories.dek: CNN reports the U.S. president has approved millions from his personal political fund for vulnerable Republicans, with one figure of about $30 million discussed, three months before midterm elections.
stories.caveman: In the United States, voters pick a president every four years. In the years in between, they pick the people who write laws. Those in-between votes are midterm elections. This November, Americans will decide who controls the two houses of Congress, the House and the Senate. If Democrats win either house, they can block President Donald Trump's plans and investigate him. Trump's own party, the Republicans, now worry they are losing. Gas is expensive. A war with Iran that Trump once said would last weeks is still going. His approval ratings are low. Advisers told CNN he has finally said yes to spending millions from his personal PAC, a big pile of campaign money, on shaky Republican races. One person mentioned $30 million as a first batch. The White House says Trump is fully committed. Trump himself recently said, 'I won. I'm not campaigning.' His team wants him to hold rallies every week in close districts, especially in Michigan, Ohio, and North Carolina, to pull out fans who vote for him but often skip midterms. They are not counting on winning over many independents.
stories.why_it_matters: Control of Congress decides whether the next two years are investigations and gridlock or a clear path for Trump's agenda, including the Iran war and spending. Republicans have also redrawn some voting maps and won a Supreme Court fight that lets party committees spend more on candidates. Democrats smell a chance if prices and the war stay ugly.
stories.camps: Republican officials say Trump is the party's leader and that border, tax-cut, and crime numbers will save them if he shows up. They also argue new district maps and extra campaign-cash rules help. Democrats say voters are angry about prices and an unpopular war, and that pouring MAGA money into base turnout is a sign the party cannot win the middle. Some Republican lawmakers privately say Trump waited too long. Trump's circle says he will not waste endorsements on 'losers.'
stories.image_alt: Donald Trump walks onstage at a rally under a Powering the American Dream banner

terms.explain: U.S. elections halfway through a president's four-year term. The whole House and about one-third of the Senate are on the ballot. The president's party often loses seats.
The U.S. law-making body. The House has 435 voting members. The Senate has 100. If the other party wins either one, the president cannot pass most laws alone.
A legal pot of money used to help candidates. Trump has a large one from his own political brand.
The larger, more local half of Congress. Every seat is up this November. It can start tax bills and impeachment.
The smaller half of Congress. Senators serve six years. It confirms judges and can block almost any bill.
The nickname for Trump's most loyal voters. Republican strategy now is to get these people to show up, not to win many swing voters.
A person who does not always vote for the same party. Trump's team thinks few of them will come back this year.
Changing the lines of voting districts. The party that draws friendly lines can win more seats with the same number of votes. Trump pushed Republicans to do this in several states.
The share of people who say the president is doing a good job. Low scores make midterms harder for his party.
A public blessing. In the GOP, Trump's endorsement can make or break a candidate. Advisers say he will not back people he thinks will lose.
A Congress process that can charge and, if the Senate agrees, remove a president. Trump faced it twice in his first term and does not want a hostile Congress again.
Rules that make people show identification to vote. Republicans in Congress fought over a Trump-backed bill on this and did not pass it.
A place where both parties have a real chance. Michigan, Ohio, and North Carolina are examples this year.
A White House spokesperson who told CNN Trump is committed to keeping the Republican majority.
Trump's top White House aide. She also helps run the midterm political operation.
The White House press secretary, who speaks to reporters for the president. She said she is leaving at the end of August, two months before the vote.

stories.headline: Iran says no new U.S. talks as Trump claims he will take Hormuz
stories.dek: Iran's foreign minister said Saturday there is no decision to restart negotiations, a day after President Trump said he would 'pretty soon' declare the Strait of Hormuz U.S. territory.
stories.caveman: The United States and Israel began bombing Iran on February 28. They said they wanted to stop a nuclear bomb and, at times, to topple Iran's leaders. The war is now in a second phase. A paper promise signed in June was supposed to lead to 60 days of talks. That window ends Monday. Almost no real talks happened. On Friday, Trump told a New York crowd that Iran is being 'very badly defeated' and that after the win he will declare the Strait of Hormuz, the oil sea lane, a territory of the United States. That would be like one country planting a flag on a busy international highway. Iran's deputy foreign minister called the idea a delusion and said the strait opens and closes only under Iran's command. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Qatar and Pakistan are passing messages, but that is not negotiation, and Tehran has not decided to sit down again. He blames Washington for breaking the June understanding. Meanwhile Israel struck southern Lebanon, and a tanker was hit in the strait. Ordinary Iranians are also paying: President Masoud Pezeshkian blamed a U.S. port blockade and lost oil sales for high inflation at home.
stories.why_it_matters: If talks stay dead, the oil chokepoint stays shut, prices stay high, and the U.S. midterms get harder for Trump's party. A claim that Hormuz is U.S. land also alarms countries that treat it as an international waterway. For East Asia, this is a politics story with a direct bill: fuel, shipping insurance, and the risk that a wider war pulls in more navies.
stories.camps: Trump says Iran is evil, is losing, and must never get a nuclear weapon, and that Americans should accept higher gas as the price. Iran says the U.S. failed to overthrow it, must accept defeat, and that Hormuz cannot be seized by a speech. Gulf Arab states want ships to move and have accused Iran of hitting tankers. European and Asian importers want a ceasefire and an open strait. Anti-war voices in the U.S. and on the left say the war has already missed its political goals and is punishing civilians and global consumers.
stories.image_alt: A small boat passes cargo ships in hazy waters near Iran

terms.explain: The narrow sea door of the Persian Gulf. It is not any one country's private driveway under normal international rules.
An agreement to stop shooting, at least for a while. It is not the same as a peace treaty, which ends a war for good.
A written political promise, weaker than a treaty. The U.S. and Iran signed one in June. Each side now says the other broke it.
Sitting down to bargain. Iran says passing notes through Qatar and Pakistan does not count as real talks with Washington.
Iran's top diplomat. On Saturday he said Tehran has not decided to restart talks with the United States.
The Iranian official who said Hormuz 'cannot be seized with a tweet' and that Iran will keep the string closed until the U.S. accepts defeat.
Iran's president. He has blamed the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, and lost oil income, for high inflation at home.
A sea lane that ships of all countries are supposed to be able to use. Trump calling Hormuz U.S. territory clashes with that idea.
Using ships and pressure to stop goods going in or out. The U.S. is squeezing Iran's ports. Iran is squeezing the strait.
A small Gulf country that hosts a big U.S. base and is trying to pass messages between Washington and Tehran. Iran also claims Qatar is holding three Iranian pilots. Qatar denies it.
Iran's neighbor, which helped with the June understanding and is still carrying messages.
An armed political group in Lebanon, backed by Iran. Israel says it is still fighting it in the south despite a June framework deal.
A sketch of a deal, not the final contract. In June, Israel and Lebanon's government outlined Israeli withdrawal in exchange for Hezbollah disarming. Hezbollah did not join the talks.
Land or water a country claims as its own. Declaring Hormuz U.S. territory would be an enormous legal and military step, not a slogan with force by itself.
Rising prices. Iran's president says the war and blockade are driving this inside Iran, just as Americans complain about gasoline.

stories.headline: Washington drafts a letter: pick America's AI club or China's
stories.dek: A U.S. State Department draft reviewed by Reuters would tell 35 countries they cannot stay in a U.S. AI coalition if they also join Beijing's rival group.
stories.caveman: The United States and China are in a race to build the smartest computers. That race needs three things: the AI programs themselves, the special chips that run them, and the rare rocks used to make those chips. Last year Washington started a club called Pax Silica to lock those three things among friends. About two dozen countries have joined, including Japan, Australia, South Korea, and Kazakhstan. In July, Chinese President Xi Jinping launched his own club, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, and pushed China's free-to-download AI models. Kazakhstan, which has important minerals, joined both. That rang alarms in Washington. Reuters saw a draft U.S. letter to 35 countries that signed a looser June 'AI Opportunity Statement.' The letter says being part of everything is being part of nothing, and that Pax Silica is a commitment, not a gym membership. It does not name China, but a U.S. official said you cannot have it both ways. The State Department would not comment on a leaked draft. It is not clear when, or if, the letter will be sent. For places like Taiwan, Japan, and Korea, this is the newest version of an old demand: choose a camp.
stories.why_it_matters: If the letter goes out, middle countries that want Chinese trade and U.S. chips will be squeezed. The U.S. hopes to starve China of minerals and partners. China will call it bloc politics. Open Chinese AI models are already popular with developers worldwide, so a hard split could also split the internet of models, not just of websites.
stories.camps: U.S. officials say a country cannot be a trusted partner in one tech system while joining a Chinese project built to compete with it. China says it is offering open cooperation and that Washington is forcing an either-or Cold War. Allies such as Japan, Australia, and South Korea are already in the U.S. club. Countries that sell minerals or want both markets, Kazakhstan first among them, will try to stall. Some U.S. companies want open Chinese models available; others want a hard wall. Left-liberal critics worry that 'choose a side' talk turns a public technology into a military alliance and ignores how concentrated power already is in a few U.S. firms.
stories.image_alt: The flags of the United States and China placed together

terms.explain: A U.S.-led club launched last year to share work on AI, computer chips, and the minerals those chips need, and to keep those supplies away from rivals.
A Chinese-led group Xi Jinping launched in July. It promotes China's open AI models as a different path from U.S. control.
A softer U.S. paper that 35 countries signed in June, saying they share a vision on AI. The draft letter goes to this larger group, not only full Pax Silica members.
The U.S. foreign ministry. It writes letters to other countries and runs embassies.
A tiny electronic brain. Modern AI needs advanced chips, many of them designed in the U.S. and made in East Asia, including Taiwan.
Metals and minerals that high-tech industry cannot easily replace. China has a tight grip on many of them and has used that grip in trade fights.
An AI whose inner numbers are published so others can download, run, and change it. Chinese firms have been strong in this category.
A government rule that says you may not sell certain goods, such as advanced chips, to certain countries.
A Central Asian country with lots of useful minerals. It is the only country known to have joined both the U.S. and Chinese AI clubs.
China's top leader. He is using AI diplomacy to offer an alternative to U.S. rules.
The path a product takes from mine to factory to phone. Whoever controls the path can squeeze everyone else.
A leading U.S. AI firm. Chinese open models have been catching up with its closed systems, which worries Washington.
Another top U.S. AI company. Together with OpenAI it stands for the closed, tightly held American model.
When big powers force smaller countries to join one team and shun the other, the way the U.S. and Soviet Union once did.
The long U.S.–Soviet standoff after World War II. People use the phrase now when Washington and Beijing split the world into two systems.

stories.headline: A big American fiction week: Lee, Obreht, and Russo's first thriller
stories.dek: Lit Hub's Friday review roundup put Chang-rae Lee and Téa Obreht at the top of the pile, while Pulitzer winner Richard Russo is out with his first thriller and talking it up this weekend.
stories.caveman: Every few weeks, American book culture has a 'new books Tuesday.' This one was heavy. Chang-rae Lee, a Korean American novelist known for careful, sad, beautiful books, published A Tender Age. It follows a 10-year-old boy through a charged summer at a Korean church camp and draws on Lee's own childhood. Reviewers this week mostly raved. Téa Obreht, who became famous young for The Tiger's Wife, published Sunrise, a layered story that plays with Old West myths, gender, and the wrecking of wild land. Critics called it riveting; one review panned it. Richard Russo, who won a Pulitzer Prize years ago for Empire Falls, a novel about a fading mill town, did something new: a thriller called Under the Falls. A thriller is a tense plot book, more 'what happens next' than 'how does this sentence feel.' Reviewers were split — some loved the mood, some did not. Russo told a public-radio interviewer on Saturday that fans of his quieter books should still give it a chance. Also in the same pile: Claire Carusillo's The Responsible Party, which the New York Times Book Review praised as comic and sharp. If you woke up from a cave, the simple map is this: the 'serious fiction' shelf is busy, and a beloved old-school realist just tried on a crime-novel coat.
stories.why_it_matters: U.S. literary fame still runs through a few review pages, public radio, and prize circuits. A week when Lee, Obreht, and Russo land together tells you who the establishment is betting on for fall conversations, book-club lists, and, later, awards. It also shows a trend: even prize-winning realists are borrowing thriller engines to keep readers.
stories.camps: This is not a left-right fight. It is a taste fight. Literary reviewers reward language, ambiguity, and social history. Thriller readers want pace. Russo is crossing that line, so some fans will follow and some will sniff. Lee and Obreht sit in the high-prestige lane that the New York Times, Booklist, and Lit Hub still anoint. Commercial romantasy, which is outselling almost all of this, lives on another planet — see the next story.

stories.headline: TikTok romantasy still rules the charts as D.C. prepares a literary festival
stories.dek: Publishers Weekly said Hannah Nicole Maehrer's fourth Evie Sage book is the top-selling title in the U.S., while the National Book Festival on August 22 will crown Ann Patchett and host a long prestige lineup.
stories.caveman: There are two American book countries right now, and they barely share a subway line. In one country, a TikTok-famous series about a young woman tangled up with a villain is eating the sales chart. Hannah Nicole Maehrer's new paperback, Adversary to the Villain, is number one in the whole country, Publishers Weekly said on August 14. That is her second book in a row to do that. The style is romantasy: romance plus fantasy, heavy on feelings, banter, and special-world rules. Riley Sager's island mystery The Unknown and Chris Bohjalian's suburban thriller The Amateur also hit the hardcover list, helped in Bohjalian's case by a Bookstagram star who also buys books for a Hollywood studio. In the other country, the Library of Congress will throw its National Book Festival in Washington on August 22. Ann Patchett, author of Bel Canto, The Dutch House, and this summer's Whistler, will receive the Library's Prize for American Fiction, a lifetime-style honor that has gone to Toni Morrison and Louise Erdrich. Patchett also owns an independent bookstore in Nashville and has become a mascot for indie shops. Whistler has lived on the New York Times bestseller list since June. So: online romantasy is who is commercially hottest. Patchett is who the official culture still taps as the American novelist of the moment.
stories.why_it_matters: Sales decide which writers get the next contract and which stories fill airport racks. Festivals and library prizes decide who gets taught, quoted, and remembered. The split explains why a reader can feel that 'nobody reads literary novels' and also that 'serious books are everywhere' — both are true in different rooms. Hollywood is watching both rooms: a Universal executive's book club just boosted Bohjalian.
stories.camps: Not a party fight, but a class-and-platform fight. Romantasy fans, many of them young and online, say gatekeepers ignored them until the money became impossible to deny. Literary institutions say a prize like the Library of Congress award is about a whole career, not one viral month. Some critics sneer at TikTok books as junk food. Some TikTok readers sneer at prize fiction as homework. A fair reading is that U.S. publishing now runs on two hit machines at once, and both are real.

stories.headline: Thousands of children sleep on Ceuta streets after a mass crossing
stories.dek: Aid groups say about 1,500 unaccompanied minors are inside Spain's protection system, but more than 4,000 may still be unidentified in the overwhelmed enclave.
stories.caveman: Ceuta is a small Spanish city on the African coast, stuck to Morocco. In late July, a huge number of people crossed the fence and the sea into this city. Many adults were sent back. Children who arrive alone are harder to return, because child-protection law is supposed to cover them first. Two weeks later, the city is still packed. Neighbors and a local group called Luna Blanca have been cooking every day; on the first day they handed out 3,500 boxes of food. Some people eat once a day. The scariest gap is kids. About 1,500 children and teenagers are already in official shelters. Save the Children, talking to Euronews on August 14, estimates more than 4,000 others have not even been identified. Some hide because they fear the centers. Unicef Spain says the shelters are full and children on the street are not safe. Amnesty International says it is gathering evidence of possible rushed, unlawful returns to Morocco, but it calls that a preliminary finding, not a finished court case. Spain and Morocco have agreed to send people back faster. Spanish regions argue about who should take the children onto the mainland. This is a child-protection emergency, not a sports story.
stories.why_it_matters: Unaccompanied children on the street face violence, trafficking, and sickness. If Europe only funds fences and not safe routes or shared shelters, the next crossing will look the same. Ceuta is tiny; the Spanish state and the EU, not one city, own the legal duty. How Spain moves, identifies, or returns these children will be a test of the 'best interests of the child' rule that governments quote and often skip.
stories.camps: Ceuta's local government says it cannot host this many people alone. Humanitarian groups want fast transfers to mainland Spain, case-by-case family checks, and no mass returns. Some Spanish regions do not want the children. Madrid is talking to Rabat about quicker repatriation. Moroccan critics say their own state also uses migration as politics. Right-wing voices talk about disorder and NGOs 'helping people leave'; the Red Cross has denied smuggling claims. A left-leaning reading puts children's safety above border optics, and still admits residents are exhausted.

terms.explain: A Spanish city on the north coast of Africa, sharing a land border with Morocco. It is part of Spain and the EU, but it is not on the European mainland.
A child who arrives in a country without a parent or legal guardian. Child-welfare law, not only immigration law, is supposed to apply.
The official shelters, social workers, and courts that must house and care for children. In Ceuta those rooms are full.
A big international charity that works for children's rights. It estimated more than 4,000 unidentified minors in Ceuta.
The United Nations children's agency. Its Spain office said many minors are still on the street and centers are saturated.
A Spanish refugee-aid group. It says unidentified children cannot get proper legal help or mental-health care.
A global human-rights group. It told Euronews it sees early signs of possible summary, unlawful returns, and is still investigating.
Sending someone back across a border without checking if they are a child, a refugee, or in danger. International law generally forbids doing this in a rush.
A legal rule: when adults decide for a child, the child's safety and future come first, ahead of migration status.
A Ceuta community group. Volunteers have been cooking daily for people sleeping outside.

stories.headline: WHO: attacks on hospitals now average more than four a day
stories.dek: From January to August 2026 the agency counted over 900 attacks on health care, with about 900 dead and 1,400 hurt, mostly in Ukraine, Lebanon, and Gaza.
stories.caveman: A hospital is supposed to be a safe building even in a war. The World Health Organization, the United Nations health office, said in Geneva on August 14 that this rule is failing. From January to August 2026 it verified more than 900 attacks on clinics, ambulances, staff, and patients. That is more than four a day. About 900 people died and more than 1,400 were hurt. Ninety-four health workers were detained. The official who presented the numbers, Altaf Musani, said the violence includes heavy weapons, wrecked buildings, and kidnapping. Ukraine, Lebanon, and the occupied Palestinian territory have the most reported incidents this year. Gaza: all 36 hospitals have been damaged, and only about half still work at all. Sudan: 37 percent of health facilities are not working. Ukraine: more than 3,100 attacks since Russia's full-scale invasion, including 156 this year, and a recent hit on a WHO warehouse. Since tracking began in 2018, the WHO has verified over 10,400 attacks in 29 countries. Musani said not one of those 10,000-plus cases has entered a real accountability process. A WHO study in northwest Syria found that after 69 attacks, clinic visits dropped by half and stayed low for more than a month. In Congo, 12 attacks since an Ebola outbreak was declared in May have made it harder to find and treat sick people.
stories.why_it_matters: When a clinic is hit, the harm lasts. Tomorrow's births, dialysis, and vaccinations disappear. Disease outbreaks spread. International law already says medical sites are protected; the new fact is that nobody is being held to account. That makes bombing hospitals cheaper, politically, than it should be.
stories.camps: The WHO presents verified counts, not a court verdict naming every culprit. Israel, Russia, Sudan's armies, and other armed groups all deny or justify strikes in their own wars. Human-rights groups say the pattern is now so common it looks like a method, not an accident. Some governments call the WHO political. A left-leaning reading treats attacks on health care as a rights crime first, and asks why 10,000 verified cases produced zero accountability, instead of arguing only about which flag is worse.

terms.explain: The United Nations agency for global health. It counts attacks on medical care in wars and tries to send supplies.
A strike, raid, detention, or other act that hits a clinic, ambulance, warehouse, health worker, or patient. The WHO only publishes cases it says it has verified.
The WHO's director of humanitarian and disaster management. He presented the 2026 numbers in Geneva on August 14.
The wartime rulebook. It says hospitals, ambulances, and medical staff must not be targets. Breaking it can be a war crime.
The WHO's name for Palestinian land under Israeli occupation, including Gaza. Gaza's 36 hospitals are all damaged, the agency said.
A real investigation and trial after a crime. The WHO said none of the 10,400-plus verified attacks since 2018 have entered one.
A deadly virus spread by body fluids. In Congo, attacks on clinics since May 2026 have disrupted the hunt for new cases.
A regular medical visit where you are not admitted overnight. In northwest Syria, these visits fell 51 percent right after attacks.

stories.headline: A 7.7 quake kills at least 47 people on Indonesia's Flores island
stories.dek: The Saturday morning shock flattened houses and public buildings. Rescuers are still searching, and officials say the count may rise.
stories.caveman: Early Saturday, August 15, before 5 a.m. local time, the ground under Flores island in eastern Indonesia jumped. The country's weather office called it magnitude 7.7, about 15 kilometers deep. Shallow quakes shake houses harder. At least 47 people were killed, Indonesia's disaster agency said as the BBC updated the story on August 16. Many died in their sleep when roofs came down, the East Nusa Tenggara governor said. The worst counts were in Manggarai (24) and East Manggarai (17), then Sikka and smaller numbers in nearby districts. More than 150 houses were badly damaged, plus schools, clinics, and places of worship. Video from Maumere port showed concrete falling on people waiting for a ferry; a gangway collapsed and some were thrown into the water. A tsunami warning sent about 2,000 people inland; it was lifted after roughly three hours when the sea did not rise in a dangerous way. Aftershocks kept people cooking outside. The disaster agency said it was sending aid and warned the death toll could grow because the area is remote and mountainous. Indonesia sits where big pieces of the Earth's crust push each other, so quakes are not rare. This one is a rescue-and-shelter story right now, not a finished reconstruction story.
stories.why_it_matters: A 7.7 quake in a poor, hilly island chain can erase homes, clinics, and a harvest in one minute. How fast Jakarta sends tents, water, and medical teams decides whether 47 becomes a much larger number from injury and disease. It is also a reminder that climate headlines are not the only disaster beat: tectonics still kill, and remote provinces often wait longer for help.
stories.camps: This is not a left-right war. The national disaster agency and the provincial governor are the official voices; local residents describe fear and outdoor sleeping. Opposition politicians in Indonesia often use slow aid to attack whoever holds Jakarta. International agencies will watch whether clinics and schools are rebuilt, not only roads for tourists near Labuan Bajo. A humanitarian reading starts with search, shelter, and the people still under rubble, before anyone talks about tourism damage.

terms.explain: A score for how strong an earthquake is. Each whole number is much more energy than the one below. 7.7 is a major quake.
An island in eastern Indonesia. The Saturday quake hit here, far from Bali, in a mountainous province.
Indonesia's national disaster office. It reports deaths, damage, and where aid is going.
An alert that a quake may push a dangerous wave onto the shore. This time the warning was lifted after about three hours.
Smaller quakes that follow a big one. They make damaged buildings more likely to fall, so people sleep outside.
The point on the Earth's surface above where the quake started. Nearby towns shake most.
Huge slabs of the Earth's crust. Indonesia sits where several meet, so quakes and volcanoes are common.
A town and port on Flores. Video showed the terminal shedding concrete onto ferry passengers.

stories.headline: SpaceX now owns Cursor, the $60 billion coding helper
stories.dek: The AI writing tool many programmers use every day is officially part of Elon Musk's rocket company, which already swallowed xAI.
stories.caveman: Imagine a helper that sits in a coder's laptop and writes software with them. That helper is called Cursor. It got so popular that SpaceX, the rocket firm run by Elon Musk, agreed to buy it for about $60 billion. The option was signed in April. SpaceX later went public. On Friday the purchase closed. Cursor's own blog said it now sits inside SpaceX. SpaceX also bought Musk's other AI firm, xAI, earlier this year. xAI makes a chatbot named Grok. Cursor says it will help build Grok and will get to use SpaceX's huge pile of computer chips, called GPUs. SpaceX already rents those chips to Anthropic and Google. There is a catch: SpaceX is being sued over dirty air from the gas turbines that power its data centers. A $60 billion price for a coding app is enormous. It means one person's companies now own rockets, a social network, a chatbot, and the tool a generation of young programmers open every morning.
stories.why_it_matters: If one company owns both the factories that train AI and the tool people use to write code, it can set prices and rules for a whole generation of software. Towns near the data centers also breathe the exhaust. Workers and smaller AI labs may find the chips they need are reserved for the house brand.
stories.camps: Musk and Cursor say this is how you scale intelligence: more chips, one roof. Critics say it is too much power in one man's hands, and that the climate bill is paid by neighbors of the turbines. Some programmers worry their favorite tool will be bent toward Grok and X. Others just want faster chips and do not care who signs the checks.
