The U.S. company that launches rockets and satellites. It went public this year and now also owns xAI and Cursor.
The billionaire who runs SpaceX, xAI, and the social app X. Critics say too many key AI tools now sit in his group.
Musk's AI company, bought by SpaceX earlier this year. It builds the Grok chatbot.
xAI's chatbot. Cursor says it will now help build it, including a new agent feature.
A kind of computer chip that is very good at the math AI needs. Owning many of them is like owning the fuel.
A warehouse full of computers. Training big AI needs huge ones, which use a lot of electricity and can pollute if they burn gas.
When one company buys another. SpaceX had an option to buy Cursor for $60 billion and used it.
When a private firm starts selling shares to ordinary investors. SpaceX did this earlier this year.
A top U.S. AI company. It is one of the customers renting SpaceX computing power.
A jet-like engine that burns fuel to make electricity. SpaceX faces a lawsuit over pollution from turbines at its data centers.
Software that does not just answer a question but takes steps on its own, like clicking and writing files.

stories.headline: Claude will hide a secret mark in the words it writes
stories.dek: Anthropic said Friday it will stamp chatbot text so schools and bosses can check if a machine wrote it. Some paying users say they will quit.
stories.caveman: A chatbot named Claude writes emails, essays, and code for millions of people. Its maker, Anthropic, said it will start putting a secret pattern in those words. The pattern is called a watermark. You cannot see it. A special key can. The company is doing this because a European Union rule, the AI Act, says AI firms must make machine writing checkable. Anthropic will use a method Google DeepMind published in 2024, called SynthID-Text. It also plans a public tool so others can test a block of text. Light edits probably will not wipe the mark. A full rewrite will. Code will carry less of a mark, because there are fewer word choices that still run. Some users on social media said they canceled. They do not want a teacher or a boss to catch them. Others said hiding AI use is just lying. Anthropic says the mark does not change quality, and that other big AI firms signed the same European code and will do this too.
stories.why_it_matters: Schools, newsrooms, and offices are drowning in machine text. A watermark is a tool, not a truth serum. If only some companies stamp and others do not, cheaters will switch apps. If the mark is easy to wash out, the rule is theater. Workers also deserve to know whether their employer will treat a stamp like a crime.
stories.camps: The EU and many teachers want labels so people know when a machine spoke. Labor and student voices say people should not be punished for using a tool their school or company also uses. Some Claude fans call the mark a snitch. Transparency advocates say the only people angry are the ones who planned to pass AI work off as their own. Both things can be partly true.
stories.image_alt: A grid of black magnifying glasses on a pale blue background, a Getty illustration used by TechCrunch

terms.explain: A hidden pattern in AI writing. A person cannot see it. A special key can prove a machine chose the words.
Anthropic's chatbot, a rival to ChatGPT. It will now watermark the text it generates.
The U.S. AI company that makes Claude. It says it is watermarking to follow an EU transparency rule.
A European Union law and follow-up code that tell AI companies to make machine-made content identifiable.
A watermarking method Google DeepMind described in 2024. Anthropic says it will use this approach.
A public computer door that lets others send text and ask, 'Is this watermarked?' Anthropic says it will release one.
A different kind of checker. It looks for writing habits common in AI, not a hidden key. Anthropic says that is not the same as a watermark.
A computer program trained on enormous amounts of text so it can write and answer in human-like language.
When two words both work, the model can pick the one that fits a secret pattern. That is how the watermark hides.
Google's main AI lab. It published the SynthID-Text idea that Anthropic is adopting.
Some paying Claude users said they would quit after the watermark news, because they do not want to be caught using it at work or school.

stories.headline: A BookTok dystopian romance hits No. 1 under an AI cloud
stories.dek: H.M. Wolfe's Daggermouth, once a self-published Kindle hit, now tops hardcover fiction after a seven-figure deal. A study flagged it. She says that is false.
stories.caveman: A love story set in a cruel future, called Daggermouth, started as a cheap ebook. Readers on TikTok — the BookTok crowd — made it huge. Simon & Schuster's new romance imprint, Scarlett Press, paid about seven figures for this book and a sequel. The new hardcover is now number one on the Publishers Weekly hardcover fiction list. At the same time, researchers at Stony Brook University ran a tool named Pangram on more than 14,000 Kindle books. They said Daggermouth scored about 60 percent machine-written, the highest among popular titles they checked, and that they found rare phrases that also show up in other suspected AI books. Wolfe, through a lawyer, said she did not use generative AI and that such tools are unreliable. She has also said she opposes AI in the writing process. The Atlantic, which reported the study, noted there is no final proof. Pangram has flagged human writing before. Simon & Schuster and the British publisher Tor Bramble say they stand behind the book. The study is not yet peer reviewed.
stories.why_it_matters: If machine-written books can win seven-figure deals and the top hardcover slot, human writers lose work and readers lose trust. If a shaky detector can wreck a career, that is another kind of harm. Publishing still has no shared rule for what 'written by a person' means.
stories.camps: Some researchers and rival authors say the signs are too strong to ignore. Wolfe and her publishers say accusation is not evidence. Romance readers mostly care whether the book moves them. Bookstores are stuck in the middle: they need the sales and they need a clean name. A fair reading holds both the study and the denial in view until someone shows real proof.
stories.image_alt: Official cover of H.M. Wolfe's Daggermouth: a grey heart and black rose bound in red cord on black

terms.explain: A dystopian enemies-to-lovers romance by H.M. Wolfe. It began as a self-published ebook and is now a hardcover number one.
The author of Daggermouth. She denies using generative AI. Her publishers have stood by her.
The book corner of TikTok. A viral video there can turn an unknown ebook into a national bestseller.
A new-adult romance imprint at Simon & Schuster, launched in 2025. It published the Daggermouth hardcover.
A contract worth at least $1 million. S&S and the U.K. house Tor Bramble paid this for Daggermouth and a sequel.
A tool that guesses whether text was written by a machine. Researchers said Daggermouth scored about 60 percent. It has also flagged human writing.
When other experts check a study before it counts as settled science. The Stony Brook paper has not had this yet.
The U.S. book trade's main magazine. Its weekly list is what editors mean by number one in the country.
A book the author puts out without a traditional house, often on Amazon. Big publishers now hunt the ones that already sold.
A U.S. magazine that reported the Stony Brook study. It also said there is no definitive proof Wolfe used AI.
The British publisher that partnered on Daggermouth and has also stood by the author.
Software that can invent sentences. The fight is whether a hit novel was made with it, and whether anyone can prove that.
The Instagram corner that poses and praises books. Together with BookTok it now moves hardcover piles.

stories.headline: Claudia Rankine's new book asks what to do when the world will not stop hurting
stories.dek: Weekend reviews of Triage, the poet's hybrid work about grief, Gaza, and two friends who cannot agree whether to collapse or keep fighting.
stories.caveman: Claudia Rankine is one of the best-known living U.S. poets. Her book Citizen made poetry a bestseller and talked about everyday racism. Her new book, Triage, came out August 4 from Graywolf Press. This weekend, papers from Dublin to New York are still arguing with it. The story is a long talk between a narrator and a friend called the theorist. They met in college. When the world felt like too much, they used to fall down on the campus grass on purpose. That drop was their way to say: we see the pain. Now they disagree. The theorist, who left Ramallah as a teen, says collapse is only useful if you get up and act. The narrator is more tired. She is not sure action still works. Reviewers say the book looks at genocide, climate, and burnout, and that it does not hand you a happy ending. Rankine has said the two people are composite characters, not a straight memoir.
stories.why_it_matters: When a famous American writer puts Gaza, grief, and protest into a mainstream book, it becomes part of how U.S. readers talk about the war and about giving up. Libraries, classrooms, and prize lists will carry that talk into the fall.
stories.camps: This is not a party-line fight so much as a fight inside the left. Activists who want bodies in the street may find the narrator too still. Readers worn out by the news may feel seen. Some reviewers wanted a clearer answer. Rankine refuses to give one. That refusal is the point, and also the thing that will annoy people who came for a slogan.
stories.image_alt: Cover of Claudia Rankine's Triage: two people sharing oversized red clothes on a yellow field

terms.explain: A major U.S. poet and critic. Citizen made her famous. Triage is her new hybrid book.
Rankine's 2026 book from Graywolf. It is part memoir, part argument, about grief and what to do in a collapsing world.
Rankine's 2014 book about everyday racism. It was a rare poetry bestseller and is taught in many U.S. schools.
An independent U.S. publisher in Minneapolis, known for poetry and serious nonfiction. It published Triage.
The friend in Triage who left Ramallah at 18. In the book they argue that collapse only matters if you get up and fight.
A city in the occupied West Bank. The theorist's leaving it is one of the book's open wounds.
Writing that is not only a novel, not only an essay, not only a poem. Rankine has worked in this mixed form for years.
A person on the page built from more than one real life. Rankine has said the speaker and the theorist are composites.
The Palestinian territory at the center of a war that hangs over Triage. Reviewers say the book keeps returning to it.
An ancient Greek play about two sisters who disagree on duty after a war. Reviewers hear that argument in Rankine's pair.
When a person is too tired to keep caring at full strength. Triage treats this as a political fact, not just a mood.

stories.headline: Washington and Ottawa are still far apart as a 50 percent tariff clock ticks
stories.dek: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Friday America will not accept Canadian retaliation. A new levy on hundreds of Canadian goods is set for August 19.
stories.caveman: The United States and Canada sell a huge amount of stuff to each other. Cars, steel, milk, beer, and wood cross the border every day. President Donald Trump has already taxed some of those goods. He now says that on August 19 he will add a 50 percent tariff on hundreds more Canadian products, on top of the old ones. A tariff is a tax on imports. It makes foreign goods more expensive. Greer, Trump's trade chief, spoke at a factory in Iowa on Friday. He said this is not a trade war, that America is protecting its own factories, and that if Canada hits back, Washington will hit harder. He compared Canada's liquor bans to something China would do. Canada's trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, has been in Washington. Prime Minister Mark Carney wants the new tax dropped and the old steel and auto taxes cut. Sources told Canadian papers the two sides are not close. Canada may settle for a small pause. Quebec's Bloc party says do not touch the dairy system that protects local farmers.
stories.why_it_matters: Canada is one of America's biggest trading partners. A 50 percent wall on everyday goods would raise prices in both countries, hurt factory towns that share one supply chain, and teach every other U.S. ally that a deal can vanish in a week.
stories.camps: Trump's team says tariffs bring factories home and punish countries that ban U.S. alcohol or fence off milk. Canadian officials and a former ambassador say America is using size as a weapon and calling self-defense illegal. Workers on both sides of the auto plants just want the line to keep moving. Dairy farmers in Quebec do not want their quota system bargained away. Shoppers in both countries will pay if the clock runs out.
stories.image_alt: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer gestures while talking on a factory floor in Des Moines, Iowa

terms.explain: A tax on goods coming in from another country. A 50 percent tariff means a $10 item can cost $15 at the border before anyone's profit.
Trump's top trade official. In Iowa on Friday he said Washington will not tolerate Canadian retaliation.
Canada's prime minister. He wants the August 19 tariff dropped and the older steel and auto taxes cut.
The Canadian minister running the talks in Washington with Greer.
A U.S. national-security trade law. Trump has used it to tax foreign steel, aluminum, cars, and lumber.
The current North American free-trade deal. Most Canadian goods that follow it have been exempt — until this new threat.
Canada's system that limits how much milk farmers produce and how much foreign milk comes in. Quebec politicians say do not touch it.
Hitting back after someone taxes you. Canada pulled some U.S. alcohol from provincial stores. Greer called that China-like.
A 1930s U.S. tariff law. Reports say Trump is using a leftover piece of it for the August 19 levy.
A Quebec party in Canada's parliament. Its leader said the U.S. has grown greedier and dairy must stay off the table.
The path a car part takes across the border, sometimes more than once, before a finished car is sold. Tariffs tax that path at every hop.
When a country buys more from abroad than it sells. Trump's team says tariffs will shrink this and pull factories home.

stories.headline: Israeli strikes kill 11 in south Lebanon, including three children
stories.dek: It is the deadliest day since a June truce. Israel says it hit a Hezbollah commander. Beirut says a family in a house was not a military target.
stories.caveman: Early Saturday, Israeli warplanes hit southern Lebanon. In the village of Ansar, a strike on a house killed seven people, including three children and two women, Lebanon's health ministry said. Later strikes on Deir al-Zahrani killed four more and wounded others. At least 11 people died. Israel said it was answering a Hezbollah attack that badly hurt three of its soldiers. It said the Ansar strike killed Ali Samir Al-Haj Hassan, a commander in Hezbollah's elite Radwan Force, and that his family was there but was not the target. Hezbollah supporters posted photos of the commander with his wife and four children and said they all died. A June deal said Israel would pull back and Hezbollah would disarm. Hezbollah never signed it. Israel still holds a strip of south Lebanon. President Joseph Aoun said the raids send a message to U.S.-led talks. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said the dead children were not military infrastructure. A spokesman for Benjamin Netanyahu said the strikes should make talks more serious, not less.
stories.why_it_matters: A truce that already leaked every day just had its bloodiest morning. If talks in Rome collapse, south Lebanon goes back to open war, and a wider Middle East fight gets another front. Children in a house should not be the price of a commander's death — or of a soldier's injury.
stories.camps: Israel says Hezbollah hides fighters among families and broke the ceasefire first. Lebanon's leaders say Israel keeps bombing homes while occupying land and calling it security. Hezbollah wants Beirut to quit U.S. talks. Human rights groups and many on the left say no targeting rule can excuse killing children; they also note Hezbollah is an armed group that chose to keep fighting. The honest picture is ugly on more than one side.
stories.image_alt: Men carry a white-shrouded body on a stretcher through a dusty wrecked street beside a crushed car

terms.explain: A village in southern Lebanon, about 70 kilometers south of Beirut. A Saturday strike on a house there killed seven people, including three children.
Another southern Lebanese town hit the same day. Lebanon said four people died there and more were wounded.
An armed political group in Lebanon, backed by Iran. It did not sign the June framework and has refused to disarm.
Hezbollah's special forces. Israel said the man it killed in Ansar commanded a battalion in this unit.
The man Israel says it killed in Ansar. His family was in the building. Hezbollah supporters say they died with him.
A June 2026 plan: Israel pulls back, Hezbollah disarms, the Lebanese army moves in. It is not a full peace treaty, and it is leaking.
An agreement to stop shooting, at least for a while. Saturday was the deadliest day since this one began in June.
Lebanon's president. He said the strikes send a clear message to the U.S.-led talks.
Lebanon's prime minister. He said the dead children and women were not military targets.
Israel's prime minister. His office said Hezbollah put civilians in a military compound and that the strikes should harden talks, not kill them.
A band of south Lebanon, about 10 kilometers deep, that Israeli forces still hold. Critics call it occupation.
When fighters stay among families so an attack on them also hits civilians. Israel used this phrase. Hezbollah called it a lie after a family died.
Direct Israel-Lebanon meetings hosted with U.S. help. An eighth round is supposed to happen in September.

stories.headline: Taliban parade on year five while 14 million Afghans go hungry
stories.dek: Kabul marked victory day on Saturday. The U.N. food agency says it can feed only one in nine people who need help, and girls are still locked out of school.
stories.caveman: Five years ago this weekend, the Taliban walked back into Kabul as U.S. forces left. On Saturday they held a parade of armored cars outside the empty old American embassy and called it victory day. Interior minister Sirajuddin Haqqani praised courage and God, and admitted some problems remain. Aid groups painted a harder picture. The World Food Programme says about 14 million Afghans are acutely hungry — one in three people — but money is so short it can feed only one in nine of them. Almost 3.7 million small children are at risk of wasting, the deadly thinness. UNESCO says about 2.5 million girls are barred from secondary school and university. U.N. Women said half of Afghan women now leave home only once or twice a month. The International Rescue Committee said needs hit a record, after drought, quakes, and neighbors pushing Afghans back from Iran and Pakistan. Only Russia has formally recognized the government. Some European countries still talk to Kabul about sending people back.
stories.why_it_matters: A forgotten war's leftover is a hunger and girls' education emergency. When rich countries cut aid and still ask the Taliban to take deportees, the bill is paid by mothers walking hours to a clinic that has no milk.
stories.camps: The Taliban say they keep order, follow their reading of Islamic law, and want trade. U.N. agencies and Afghan women say the country is being starved of both food and futures. Some Western governments argue talking to Kabul is the only way to deliver aid. Rights groups say recognition and deportation deals reward a system that erased women from public life. Ordinary families are not in any of those rooms. They are trying to find food.
stories.image_alt: A woman in a headscarf looks back while carrying a baby in a basket and walking with two girls on a mountain path

terms.explain: The armed Islamist movement that took Afghanistan back in August 2021. It is still not recognized by most countries.
The U.N. agency that feeds people in crises. In Afghanistan it can now reach only one in nine of the 14 million who are acutely hungry.
When a person does not have enough food right now, not just a poor diet. About 14 million Afghans are in this state.
When a child's body becomes dangerously thin. It is the deadliest form of malnutrition. WFP says it is critical in a third of Afghan provinces.
The U.N. education and culture agency. It says about 2.5 million Afghan girls are barred from secondary school and university.
The U.N. agency for women's rights. It said half of Afghan women now leave home only once or twice a month.
A big aid group. On Friday it said Afghanistan's humanitarian needs have reached a record.
The Taliban's interior minister. In a victory-day video he praised courage and God, and admitted problems remain.
When one country officially accepts another government as legal. Only Russia has done this for the Taliban so far.
Sending people back against their will. Iran and Pakistan have pushed millions of Afghans home, adding mouths to a hungry country.
Religious law. The Taliban say their rules on women follow it. Rights groups say the rules erase women from public life.
When donors promise less money than a crisis needs. Afghanistan's 2026 U.N. appeal was only about a quarter funded.

glossary.explain: The return on lending to Japan's government for five years. It has jumped as people bet on rate hikes.
Lee's new novel about a Korean American boy at a church camp. Published by Riverhead. Critics this week called it luminous.
Iran's top diplomat. On Saturday he said Tehran has not decided to restart talks with the United States.
A real investigation and trial after a crime. The WHO said none of the 10,400-plus verified attacks since 2018 have entered one.
When one company buys another. SpaceX had an option to buy Cursor for $60 billion and used it.
When a person does not have enough food right now, not just a poor diet. About 14 million Afghans are in this state.
The state oil company of Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates. One of its tankers was attacked in Hormuz on Friday.
The new paperback in Maehrer's series. Evie Sage has gone from assistant to adversary. A fifth book is already being guessed at.
Smaller quakes that follow a big one. They make damaged buildings more likely to fall, so people sleep outside.
Software that does not just answer a question but takes steps on its own, like clicking and writing files.
A softer U.S. paper that 35 countries signed in June, saying they share a vision on AI. The draft letter goes to this larger group, not only full Pax Silica members.
When donors promise less money than a crisis needs. Afghanistan's 2026 U.N. appeal was only about a quarter funded.
The man Israel says it killed in Ansar. His family was in the building. Hezbollah supporters say they died with him.
A huge Chinese internet company, a bit like Amazon plus a cloud-computing firm. Its AI family is called Qwen.
The WHO's director of humanitarian and disaster management. He presented the 2026 numbers in Geneva on August 14.
A global human-rights group. It told Euronews it sees early signs of possible summary, unlawful returns, and is still investigating.
A bestselling U.S. novelist and independent bookseller. She will receive the 2026 Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction at the festival.
A village in southern Lebanon, about 70 kilometers south of Beirut. A Saturday strike on a house there killed seven people, including three children.
Another top U.S. AI company. Together with OpenAI it stands for the closed, tightly held American model.
When a powerful company uses its position to block rivals, not just to make a better product. That can be illegal under U.S. law.
An ancient Greek play about two sisters who disagree on duty after a war. Reviewers hear that argument in Rankine's pair.
The only official place to download apps on an iPhone. Apple sets the rules and usually takes a cut of sales.
Apple's brand name for on-phone AI features such as writing tools and a smarter Siri.
The share of people who say the president is doing a good job. Low scores make midterms harder for his party.
A strike, raid, detention, or other act that hits a clinic, ambulance, warehouse, health worker, or patient. The WHO only publishes cases it says it has verified.
Another big Chinese tech company, best known for search. Reuters has said some of its technology may also sit inside Apple's China AI.
Japan's central bank. It sets the country's main interest rate, the way the Fed does in the United States.
The unit used to sell oil. One barrel is 42 U.S. gallons, or about 159 liters.
One-hundredth of 1 percent. If a bond yield rises 5 basis points, it went from, say, 4.68 percent to 4.73 percent.
A place where both parties have a real chance. Michigan, Ohio, and North Carolina are examples this year.
Israel's prime minister. His office said Hezbollah put civilians in a military compound and that the strikes should harden talks, not kill them.
A legal rule: when adults decide for a child, the child's safety and future come first, ahead of migration status.
When big powers force smaller countries to join one team and shun the other, the way the U.S. and Soviet Union once did.
A Quebec party in Canada's parliament. Its leader said the U.S. has grown greedier and dairy must stay off the table.
When ships or missiles stop other ships from going in or out of a port or sea lane. It is a way to choke an enemy's trade without occupying the land.
Indonesia's national disaster office. It reports deaths, damage, and where aid is going.
The informal set of novels groups of readers pick after Labor Day. A strong August review week is how books get on those lists.
The corner of Instagram where people pose and praise books. A big account can now move hardcover sales the way a newspaper review once did.
The book corner of TikTok. A viral video there can turn an unknown ebook into a national bestseller.
A standard type of oil used to set world prices. When people say 'oil is at $88,' they often mean Brent.
When a person is too tired to keep caring at full strength. Triage treats this as a political fact, not just a mood.
Borrowing cheap yen and investing the money in higher-paying assets elsewhere. When Japan raises rates, this trade can unwind fast and shake markets.
A Spanish refugee-aid group. It says unidentified children cannot get proper legal help or mental-health care.
An agreement to stop shooting, at least for a while. It is not the same as a peace treaty, which ends a war for good.
A Spanish city on the north coast of Africa, sharing a land border with Morocco. It is part of Spain and the EU, but it is not on the European mainland.
A Korean American novelist. His new book A Tender Age is getting some of the strongest U.S. reviews this week.
The official shelters, social workers, and courts that must house and care for children. In Ceuta those rooms are full.
A long-running U.S. novelist. His new book The Amateur, about a life-changing accident at a golf club, debuted on the hardcover fiction list.
Rankine's 2014 book about everyday racism. It was a rare poetry bestseller and is taught in many U.S. schools.
Author of The Responsible Party, a new novel the New York Times Book Review praised this month as funny and stylish.
Anthropic's chatbot, a rival to ChatGPT. It will now watermark the text it generates.
A major U.S. poet and critic. Citizen made her famous. Triage is her new hybrid book.
The long U.S.–Soviet standoff after World War II. People use the phrase now when Washington and Beijing split the world into two systems.
The slice of money Apple wants from a sale. Fifteen percent means Apple keeps $15 of every $100 you spend.
A person on the page built from more than one real life. Rankine has said the speaker and the theorist are composites.
The U.S. law-making body. The House has 435 voting members. The Senate has 100. If the other party wins either one, the president cannot pass most laws alone.
A poll that asks regular people how they feel about their money and the future. A falling score means people are worried.
When someone ignores a judge's order. Epic says Apple did this with the 27 percent fee and harsh link rules. That question is still alive.
A required test in China. The model must refuse or reframe answers the state does not want, for example on politics or history.
Price rises after you take out food and energy, which jump around a lot. The Fed watches this to see the deeper trend.
Metals and minerals that high-tech industry cannot easily replace. China has a tight grip on many of them and has used that grip in trade fights.
When a government spends huge sums to buy or sell its own money, hoping to change the exchange rate. Japan and the U.S. did this together last month.
A popular app that helps people write computer code with an AI sitting beside them. SpaceX just finished buying it.
The current North American free-trade deal. Most Canadian goods that follow it have been exempt — until this new threat.
The government office that decides which AI chatbots may go live in China. It registered Apple's service in July.
A dystopian enemies-to-lovers romance by H.M. Wolfe. It began as a self-published ebook and is now a hardcover number one.
A warehouse full of computers. Training big AI needs huge ones, which use a lot of electricity and can pollute if they burn gas.
Another southern Lebanese town hit the same day. Lebanon said four people died there and more were wounded.
Sending people back against their will. Iran and Pakistan have pushed millions of Afghans home, adding mouths to a hungry country.
A public computer door that lets others send text and ask, 'Is this watermarked?' Anthropic says it will release one.
A person or company that writes apps. They have long complained that Apple's cut is too high.
A score that shows whether the U.S. dollar is strong or weak against other currencies. A weaker dollar can make imports cost more.
The Canadian minister running the talks in Washington with Greer.
Using both Apple's own model and Chinese partner models at once, so Apple can pass rules and still keep some control.
A deadly virus spread by body fluids. In Congo, attacks on clinics since May 2026 have disrupted the hunt for new cases.
The billionaire who runs SpaceX, xAI, and the social app X. Critics say too many key AI tools now sit in his group.
Russo's 2001 novel about a dying New England mill town. It is the book that made him famous.
A public blessing. In the GOP, Trump's endorsement can make or break a candidate. Advisers say he will not back people he thinks will lose.
A U.S. game company that sued Apple. It wanted players to pay Epic directly instead of through Apple.
The point on the Earth's surface above where the quake started. Nearby towns shake most.
A European Union law and follow-up code that tell AI companies to make machine-made content identifiable.
How many yen one dollar buys. Near 160, many traders expect Tokyo to step in again.
A government rule that says you may not sell certain goods, such as advanced chips, to certain countries.
A button inside an app that sends you to a website to pay. Apple used to ban these. A court said it cannot.
The main bank of the United States. It does not serve regular customers. Its job is to keep prices from rising too fast and to keep as many people working as it can.
An island in eastern Indonesia. The Saturday quake hit here, far from Bali, in a mountainous province.
A sketch of a deal, not the final contract. In June, Israel and Lebanon's government outlined Israeli withdrawal in exchange for Hezbollah disarming. Hezbollah did not join the talks.
A jet-like engine that burns fuel to make electricity. SpaceX faces a lawsuit over pollution from turbines at its data centers.
The fuel most U.S. cars burn. Americans talk about the price per gallon the way others talk about the price of rice.
An editor, critic, or prize jury who decides what counts as serious. Romantasy readers say these people missed the actual audience.
The Palestinian territory at the center of a war that hangs over Triage. Reviewers say the book keeps returning to it.
A huge adding-up of everything a country makes and sells in a year. If GDP shrinks, that is a recession.
Software that creates new text, pictures, or code instead of just finding old files. ChatGPT is the famous example.
A metal people buy when they are scared of war, inflation, or messy politics. Its price often rises when other assets look risky.
Google's main AI lab. It published the SynthID-Text idea that Anthropic is adopting.
Google's app shop for Android phones. It also charges for some outside-link sales, which Apple used as a comparison.
A kind of computer chip that is very good at the math AI needs. Owning many of them is like owning the fuel.
An independent U.S. publisher in Minneapolis, known for poetry and serious nonfiction. It published Triage.
xAI's chatbot. Cursor says it will now help build it, including a new agent feature.
The author of Daggermouth. She denies using generative AI. Her publishers have stood by her.
A U.S. author whose villain-romance series is a TikTok smash. Her fourth book, Adversary to the Villain, is the country's top seller this week.
The stiff-cover first edition. Hitting this list still signals prestige, even when paperbacks sell more copies.
An armed political group in Lebanon, backed by Iran. Israel says it is still fighting it in the south despite a June framework deal.
The larger, more local half of Congress. Every seat is up this November. It can start tax bills and impeachment.
When fighters stay among families so an attack on them also hits civilians. Israel used this phrase. Hezbollah called it a lie after a family died.
Writing that is not only a novel, not only an essay, not only a poem. Rankine has worked in this mixed form for years.
A Congress process that can charge and, if the Senate agrees, remove a president. Trump faced it twice in his first term and does not want a hostile Congress again.
Buying something while you are already inside an app, like extra storage or a magazine month.
A bookshop not owned by a chain. Patchett co-owns Parnassus in Nashville and often speaks up for these stores.
A person who does not always vote for the same party. Trump's team thinks few of them will come back this year.
When the same basket of food, rent, and fuel costs more than it did last year. A little inflation is normal. A lot of it hurts people who live on wages.
What people think prices will do next year. If they expect more inflation, they may demand higher wages, which can make inflation real.
The extra money you pay to borrow. If the Fed raises this rate, mortgages, car loans, and credit cards get more expensive.
When a central bank makes borrowing more expensive on purpose, to cool prices or support its currency.
The wartime rulebook. It says hospitals, ambulances, and medical staff must not be targets. Breaking it can be a war crime.
A big aid group. On Friday it said Afghanistan's humanitarian needs have reached a record.
A sea lane that ships of all countries are supposed to be able to use. Trump calling Hormuz U.S. territory clashes with that idea.
The operating system that runs iPhones and iPads. Apple controls it tightly.
When a private firm starts selling shares to ordinary investors. SpaceX did this earlier this year.
A yearly meeting of central bankers in Wyoming, U.S. The Fed chair often gives a speech there that moves markets. This year's meeting is August 27 to 29.
Trump's top trade official. In Iowa on Friday he said Washington will not tolerate Canadian retaliation.
The number-two person in the U.S. government. He has been told to lead talks to end the Iran war and has said cheap oil is his top goal.
Alibaba's chairman. In 2025 he said Apple chose Alibaba after talking to several Chinese firms.
Lebanon's president. He said the strikes send a clear message to the U.S.-led talks.
The White House press secretary, who speaks to reporters for the president. She said she is leaving at the end of August, two months before the vote.
A Central Asian country with lots of useful minerals. It is the only country known to have joined both the U.S. and Chinese AI clubs.
The Iranian official who said Hormuz 'cannot be seized with a tweet' and that Iran will keep the string closed until the U.S. accepts defeat.
The head of the Bank of Japan. He has said the bank might speed up rate rises if money is still too easy.
The current head of the Federal Reserve. He has not clearly said whether rates will go up in September.
Another high-status U.S. publisher. It published Russo's thriller.
A company that watches oil ships from space and port data. Analysts use it to see if oil is actually moving.
A computer program trained on enormous amounts of text so it can write, translate, and answer questions in human-like language.
The U.S. national library, in Washington. It also names a poet laureate and hands out this fiction prize.

glossary.term: Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction
glossary.explain: A career prize, not a prize for one book. Past winners include Toni Morrison, Don DeLillo, Louise Erdrich, and Jesmyn Ward.
A U.S. books website that collects reviews and sets a lot of literary-internet conversation. Its Friday 'best reviewed' list is a status marker.
When two words both work, the model can pick the one that fits a secret pattern. That is how the watermark hides.
A Ceuta community group. Volunteers have been cooking daily for people sleeping outside.
The nickname for Trump's most loyal voters. Republican strategy now is to get these people to show up, not to win many swing voters.
A score for how strong an earthquake is. Each whole number is much more energy than the one below. 7.7 is a major quake.
Canada's prime minister. He wants the August 19 tariff dropped and the older steel and auto taxes cut.
Iran's president. He has blamed the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, and lost oil income, for high inflation at home.
A town and port on Flores. Video showed the terminal shedding concrete onto ferry passengers.
A written promise that is not quite a full treaty. The U.S. and Iran signed one in June. A 60-day talk window from that deal ends Monday with little progress.
U.S. elections halfway through a president's four-year term. The whole House and about one-third of the Senate are on the ballot. The president's party often loses seats.
A free, huge public book fair in Washington, D.C., run by the Library of Congress. This year's is Saturday, August 22.
Lebanon's prime minister. He said the dead children and women were not military targets.
Sitting down to bargain. Iran says passing notes through Qatar and Pakistan does not count as real talks with Washington.
The Goldilocks interest rate that neither heats up nor cools down the economy. Japan's officials think theirs sits somewhere between about 1.1 and 2.5 percent.
The most famous U.S. sales ranking. Being on it, especially at number one, is a career event.
The most powerful U.S. book-review section. A good notice there can move sales and prizes.
A bomb that uses splitting or fusing atoms. It can destroy a city. The U.S. says it went to war to stop Iran from building one. Iran says it does not want one.
The WHO's name for Palestinian land under Israeli occupation, including Gaza. Gaza's 36 hospitals are all damaged, the agency said.
A White House spokesperson who told CNN Trump is committed to keeping the Republican majority.
When the AI runs on your phone instead of a faraway server. Apple likes this for privacy. In China, the exact setup is not fully public.
An AI whose inner numbers are published so others can download, run, and change it. Chinese firms have been strong in this category.
The U.S. company behind ChatGPT. Its models are not allowed as a public service in mainland China.
A regular medical visit where you are not admitted overnight. In northwest Syria, these visits fell 51 percent right after attacks.
A legal pot of money used to help candidates. Trump has a large one from his own political brand.
Iran's neighbor, which helped with the June understanding and is still carrying messages.
A review that dislikes the book. Obreht and Russo each got at least one this week.
A different kind of checker. It looks for writing habits common in AI, not a hidden key. Anthropic says that is not the same as a watermark.
A U.S.-led club launched last year to share work on AI, computer chips, and the minerals those chips need, and to keep those supplies away from rivals.
When other experts check a study before it counts as settled science. The Stony Brook paper has not had this yet.
A measure of what companies pay for goods before they sell them to you. If this jumps, store prices often follow.
What factories pay for inputs. Japan is watching these, plus what people expect future prices to do.
An AI a company owns and trains itself, rather than renting someone else's. Apple is the first foreign firm China has cleared to offer one.
The U.S. book trade's main magazine. Its weekly bestseller list is what bookstores and editors mean by 'number one in the country.'
A set of top U.S. prizes for books, plays, and journalism. Winning one for fiction can define a career.
A small Gulf country that hosts a big U.S. base and is trying to pass messages between Washington and Tehran. Iran also claims Qatar is holding three Iranian pilots. Qatar denies it.
Alibaba's public AI model. Apple had already said it would use Qwen inside China-version Apple Intelligence.
Hezbollah's special forces. Israel said the man it killed in Ansar commanded a battalion in this unit.
A city in the occupied West Bank. The theorist's leaving it is one of the book's open wounds.
A review that loves the book. Lit Hub tallies raves versus pans so you can see the critical weather at a glance.
A writer who aims at everyday life and ordinary speech rather than magic or extreme plot twists. Russo built his name as one.
When one country officially accepts another government as legal. Only Russia has done this for the Taliban so far.
Changing the lines of voting districts. The party that draws friendly lines can win more seats with the same number of votes. Trump pushed Republicans to do this in several states.
A monthly count of how much money people in a country spend in stores and online. If the number falls, it often means households are nervous or poorer.
Hitting back after someone taxes you. Canada pulled some U.S. alcohol from provincial stores. Greer called that China-like.
An American novelist famous for small-town stories. He won the Pulitzer Prize for Empire Falls. Under the Falls is his first thriller.
A pen name for a U.S. thriller writer. His tenth novel, The Unknown, is a closed-circle mystery on a New England island and is high on the hardcover list.
A prestige imprint, meaning a named line inside a big publisher, known for literary fiction. It published Lee's new novel.
A mash-up of love story and magic-world fantasy. It is the hottest commercial genre in the U.S. right now, especially on TikTok.
Direct Israel-Lebanon meetings hosted with U.S. help. An eighth round is supposed to happen in September.
A list of 500 big U.S. companies. When people say 'the market hit a record,' they often mean this list went higher than ever.
A big international charity that works for children's rights. It estimated more than 4,000 unidentified minors in Ceuta.
A new-adult romance imprint at Simon & Schuster, launched in 2025. It published the Daggermouth hardcover.
The U.S. official in charge of government money and many sanctions. He has promised new financial pressure on Iran.
A U.S. national-security trade law. Trump has used it to tax foreign steel, aluminum, cars, and lumber.
A band of south Lebanon, about 10 kilometers deep, that Israeli forces still hold. Critics call it occupation.
A book the author puts out without a traditional house, often on Amazon. Big publishers now hunt the ones that already sold.
A tiny electronic brain. Modern AI needs advanced chips, many of them designed in the U.S. and made in East Asia, including Taiwan.
The smaller half of Congress. Senators serve six years. It confirms judges and can block almost any bill.
The part of Apple that makes money from the App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, and similar, not from selling hardware.
A contract worth at least $1 million. S&S and the U.K. house Tor Bramble paid this for Daggermouth and a sequel.
Religious law. The Taliban say their rules on women follow it. Rights groups say the rules erase women from public life.
The Taliban's interior minister. In a victory-day video he praised courage and God, and admitted problems remain.
The voice helper on iPhones. Apple Intelligence is meant to make it much smarter.
Apple's cheaper track for smaller app makers. Under the new plan they would pay 5 percent on outside-link sales.
A 1930s U.S. tariff law. Reports say Trump is using a leftover piece of it for the August 19 levy.
The U.S. company that launches rockets and satellites. It went public this year and now also owns xAI and Cursor.
The U.S. foreign ministry. It writes letters to other countries and runs embassies.
Extra-cheap or extra-plentiful money that a central bank pumps out to get people spending. Japan ran a huge version of this for about a decade and started exiting in 2024.
A narrow sea passage at the mouth of the Persian Gulf. Before the war, about one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil and a lot of gas went through it.
Some paying Claude users said they would quit after the watermark news, because they do not want to be caught using it at work or school.
When a monthly or yearly payment rolls over. Apple now says it would take 10 percent on those if you pay off-store.
Sending someone back across a border without checking if they are a child, a refugee, or in danger. International law generally forbids doing this in a rush.
Obreht's new book. Reviewers say it uses and twists Old West adventure stories and talks about gender, forbidden love, and ruined wilderness.
The path a product takes from mine to factory to phone. Whoever controls the path can squeeze everyone else.
Canada's system that limits how much milk farmers produce and how much foreign milk comes in. Quebec politicians say do not touch it.
The highest court in the United States. Its nine justices can stop or allow lower-court fights. On Thursday it refused to pause this one.
Trump's top White House aide. She also helps run the midterm political operation.
A watermarking method Google DeepMind described in 2024. Anthropic says it will use this approach.
The armed Islamist movement that took Afghanistan back in August 2021. It is still not recognized by most countries.
A giant ship built to carry oil or other bulk goods. Hitting one can spill fuel and scare other ships away.
A tax on goods coming in from another country. A 50 percent tariff means a $10 item can cost $15 at the border before anyone's profit.
Huge slabs of the Earth's crust. Indonesia sits where several meet, so quakes and volcanoes are common.
Land or water a country claims as its own. Declaring Hormuz U.S. territory would be an enormous legal and military step, not a slogan with force by itself.
A U.S. magazine that reported the Stony Brook study. It also said there is no definitive proof Wolfe used AI.
The friend in Triage who left Ramallah at 18. In the book they argue that collapse only matters if you get up and fight.
A story built to make you anxious about what happens next, often with danger or a crime. It is a genre, like romance or science fiction.
The late Nobel Prize-winning American novelist. Naming her as a past winner is how the Library tells you this prize is meant to be canonical.
The British publisher that partnered on Daggermouth and has also stood by the author.
When a country buys more from abroad than it sells. Trump's team says tariffs will shrink this and pull factories home.
A larger, nicer paperback than a cheap mass-market one. Many romantasy hits launch in this format.
A radio box on a ship that tells the world where it is. Some ships turn it off to sneak through dangerous waters.
The return you get for lending money to the U.S. government. When yields rise, borrowing gets costlier for everyone.
Rankine's 2026 book from Graywolf. It is part memoir, part argument, about grief and what to do in a collapsing world.
An alert that a quake may push a dangerous wave onto the shore. This time the warning was lifted after about three hours.
A novelist who won huge praise for The Tiger's Wife more than a decade ago. Her new novel is Sunrise.

glossary.term: U.S. District Court of Northern California
glossary.explain: The trial court in San Francisco's region that has been hearing the Epic case for years.
The U.N. agency for women's rights. It said half of Afghan women now leave home only once or twice a month.
A child who arrives in a country without a parent or legal guardian. Child-welfare law, not only immigration law, is supposed to apply.
Russo's new Knopf novel. It is darker and more plot-driven than his usual work. Reviews are mixed.
The U.N. education and culture agency. It says about 2.5 million Afghan girls are barred from secondary school and university.
The United Nations children's agency. Its Spain office said many minors are still on the street and centers are saturated.
Rules that make people show identification to vote. Republicans in Congress fought over a Trump-backed bill on this and did not pass it.
When a child's body becomes dangerously thin. It is the deadliest form of malnutrition. WFP says it is critical in a third of Afghan provinces.
A hidden pattern in AI writing. A person cannot see it. A special key can prove a machine chose the words.
The main U.S. oil price marker. It usually sits a few dollars below Brent.
Patchett's latest novel, out this summer. A woman reconnects with her stepfather. It debuted at number one on the New York Times list and is still there.
A Chinese-led group Xi Jinping launched in July. It promotes China's open AI models as a different path from U.S. control.
The U.N. agency that feeds people in crises. In Afghanistan it can now reach only one in nine of the 14 million who are acutely hungry.
The United Nations agency for global health. It counts attacks on medical care in wars and tries to send supplies.
Musk's AI company, bought by SpaceX earlier this year. It builds the Grok chatbot.
China's top leader. He is using AI diplomacy to offer an alternative to U.S. rules.
Japan's money. If it takes more yen to buy one U.S. dollar, the yen is weak. A weak yen makes foreign goods cost more in Japan.
